newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Strong wages reduce Australian rate cut chances.
newsitem.headline: Strong wages reduce Australian rate cut chances.

text.p: The odds on another Australian rate cut lengthened considerably on Thursday with the release of strong wages growth.
Average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) rose 1.2 percent in the three months to November, at the top end of expectations which had centred on a 0.9 percent rise.

In annual terms, wages growth was at 3.9 percent, again at the top end of expectations. It was also above the annual rate in August of 3.8 percent, the first time since August 1995 that the annual pace of wages growth has risen.
"The average weekly earnings report has come close to eliminating the chance of another rate cut," UBS Australian chief economist Stephen Roberts said.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) cut rates three times in the second half of 1996, reducing the official cash rate by 150 basis points to its current level of 6.0 percent.
While the wages growth was at the high end of expectations, it was not a level that was yet a threat to inflation, something economists were quick to point out.
"It doesn't change the inflation outlook in anyway," SBC Warburg senior economist Guy Bruten said.
"I think it keeps wages chugging along at four percent a year which is still consistent with inflation at around two to 2.5 percent," he said.

Others agreed, saying it was not so much the wages data that was preventing another easing, but emerging signs that the real economy was beginning to strengthen. If this proved to be a false start, then another rate cut could be delivered.

"While the inflation and wages outlook do not stand in the way of further interest rate cuts, it is the strength of the real economy that will be the key," Bankers Trust Australia senior economist Peter Munckton said.
But some did see some potential concerns on the wages front. The annual rate is currently being held down by an unusally low 0.4 percent increase in the first quarter of 1996.

That figure drops out of annual calculations in the next set of wages data, and if the first quarter figure comes in at around 1.0 percent, which analysts said was not an unreasonable forecast, then annual wages growth would rise to 4.5 percent.
An annual rate of 4.5 percent is seen by economists as the RBA's "line in the sand" beyond which wages growth is seen as posing a threat to low inflation.
The RBA aims to keep the underlying inflation rate to an average of between two and three percent over a run of years.

Adding to the concern on the wages front is the Australian Council of Trade Unions' "living wage" claim currently before the Industrial Relations Commission, which asks for low-paid workers to receive an 8.75 percent increase in award rates and three A$20 (US$15) a week safety net rises over three years.
The government has branded the claim "irresponsible".
The RBA estimated the claim would add 1.6 percentage points in wages growth, taking the annual rate to well over five percent even before flow-on effects of the claim to other sectors were seen.
National Australia Bank senior economist Jeff Oughton said that the low point in wages growth may have occured late in 1996.
"As the economy picks up through the course of 1997, and as the 'living wage' rise flows through, this is something for the market to refocus on," he said.
